extracted.intended_audience: academic researchers in finance/economics studying climate risks and asset pricing
extracted.subtask_description: The paper develops a theoretical model linking temperature (climate) risks to asset prices and implements empirical tests estimating equity exposure (betas) to temperature trends and the cross-sectional price (risk premia) of those exposures using US and international data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperature beta estimation (time-series regression)
rubrics_metrics.description:
Estimate equity exposure to temperature risks by regressing portfolio excess returns on temperature variations controlling for market and consumption growth risks: re_{i,t} = 
    5r_i +   (Eq. 19)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include the K-year moving-average change in temperature (94T^K_t), the market excess return (re_{M,t}) and the innovation in smoothed aggregate consumption growth (_C,t) as controls. Vary horizon K (1	to	10) to separate short-run (weather) vs low-frequency (global warming) components. Use first-differences of trailing moving averages to avoid look-ahead bias and estimation error; results robust to HP-filter-based trend construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of horizon K (distinguish short-run vs long-run temperature risks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use K-year trailing moving averages with K ranging from 1 to 10: K=1 captures annual/short-run (weather) fluctuations; large K captures low-frequency (global-warming) temperature trends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long-horizon (K>1) measures isolate trend/global warming effects; short-horizon (K=1) mostly captures weather. Report results across multiple K to show frequency dependence. The paper emphasizes low-frequency effects as most relevant to priced climate risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controls for market and consumption risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Control for market risk (CRSP value-weighted excess return) and macro growth risk (innovation in smoothed per-capita consumption growth) in time-series regressions of returns on temperature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motivated by CAPM and consumption-based CAPM frameworks; avoid adding ad-hoc empirical factors. These controls capture alternative sources of return variation that might confound temperature exposures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of temperature factor (moving-average vs HP filter; first differences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct temperature exposures using de-meaned changes in K-year moving-average trends; alternative: use Hodrick-Prescott filter-based trend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer one-sided trailing moving-average first-differences because they are observable and not subject to look-ahead bias; HP-filter results are similar but HP is two-sided (uses future data). Also possible to use innovations in trailing moving-average instead of first differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry classification and portfolio construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct industry portfolios and classify industries into high and low heat-exposure groups following NIOSH and Graff Zivin & Neidell (2014); use standard 25 size/book-to-market portfolios from Kenneth French for cross-section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High heat-exposure industries: mining, oil & gas extraction, construction, transportation, utilities. Low exposure: manufacturing, wholesale, retail, services, communications. Exclude agricultural (too few public firms) and financial sectors (excluded).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-sectional regression to estimate price of temperature risk (Fama-MacBeth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate the price of temperature risks by regressing average excess returns across portfolios on estimated temperature betas, controlling for market and consumption betas; use Fama-MacBeth procedure and Shanken (1992)-corrected standard errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report both standard Fama-MacBeth t-statistics and Shanken-corrected t-statistics to account for estimation error in betas. Use extended asset menus (25 portfolios plus industry portfolios) for robustness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monte Carlo simulation for inference under the null
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct Monte Carlo null distribution by simulating temperature series of matching sample size, estimating betas on simulated series, and running cross-sectional regressions; repeat 10,000 times to form distribution of t-statistics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Monte Carlo distribution to compute p-value* as fraction of simulated Shanken-corrected t-statistics less than the sample statistic. This checks that observed pricing would be unlikely under no temperature effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time-varying risk price parameterization (lambda_t linear in temperature level)
rubrics_metrics.description:
Parameterize the conditional price of temperature risk as: 
    t = 94T + T �b7 94T �b7 T_t (Eq. 20), allowing the price to depend on the temperature level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate via two-step approach: first run time-series regressions with interaction term T_{t-1} �b7 94T_t to capture conditional exposures (Eq. 21), then cross-sectionally estimate prices on the set of betas (including the interaction beta). Test whether both constant and time-varying components are significant and negative at long horizons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel regression of price-dividend ratios on temperature using Arellano-Bond GMM
rubrics_metrics.description:
Estimate dynamic panel regressions of log price-dividend ratios on K-year moving-average local temperature and macro controls: v_{i,t} = 
    5v_i + K T^K_{i,t} + ' x X_{i,t} + _v v_{i,t-1} + _{i,t} (Eq. 22), using Arellano & Bond GMM on first-differenced data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use two global price-dividend principal components to control for global macro risks and local controls (inflation, unemployment, real interest rate, GDP growth). Use White robust variance estimator. Interpret coefficient K as semi-elasticity of asset prices to temperature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of price-dividend ratio as proxy for wealth-to-consumption
rubrics_metrics.description: Use log price-dividend (or price-consumption) ratios as market proxies for the wealth-to-consumption ratio when mapping theory to data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justify with literature showing price-dividend factors capture expected growth and macroeconomic uncertainty (e.g., Jagannathan & Marakani). Use principal components of price-dividend ratios to control for common global macro factors in panel regressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orthogonalization of short- and long-run temperature components
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate long-run (LR^K_{i,t} = K-year moving-average) and short-run (SR_{i,t} = annual orthogonalized wrt LR) temperature variations and include both in regressions to identify their separate effects (Eq. 23).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Orthogonalize to avoid collinearity and to attribute effects properly. Empirical finding: LR (low-frequency) effects are the dominant channel; SR effects small and often insignificant once LR is controlled for.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel VAR to estimate joint dynamics and impulse responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate a panel VAR with Yi,t = (T^8_{i,t}, T_{i,t}, v_{i,t})' and global controls to recover impulse responses of equity prices to shocks in trend and annual temperature (Eq. 24).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include country fixed effects and price-dividend global controls. Use 8-year moving average to capture low-frequency trend. Plot impulse responses with two-standard-error bands to assess persistence and significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data selection and construction (US and international datasets)
rubrics_metrics.description: US: 25 size/book-to-market portfolios and industry portfolios, CRSP value-weighted market, per-capita real consumption (NIPA), NOAA contiguous-US temperature, annual data 1934-2014. Global: 39 countries, Berkeley Earth land-surface temperature anomaly (relative to 1951-1980), price-dividend from Global Financial Data, country macro data from World Bank (1980-2009), sample 1970-2012 for temperatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document sample spans and data sources clearly; note limitations (e.g., international sample tilted towards developed economies, agricultural sector excluded due to thin public-firm listing). Use consistent units (deg F for US, deg C anomaly for global) and convert/interpret elasticities appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excess return construction and leverage adjustment
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct excess returns by subtracting the CRSP risk-free rate from portfolio returns. When interpreting price responses, account for market leverage (e.g., leverage around three) to map price-consumption ratio responses into equity price responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report both consumption-claim price changes and implied equity-price changes after applying plausible leverage factors; clarify the transformation and its quantitative implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robustness checks and time-variation analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess robustness to alternative temperature trend constructions (HP filter vs trailing moving-average), alternative horizon choices, additional controls, and subsample/overlapping-sample analyses to detect time-variation in elasticities and premiums.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use overlapping samples (e.g., 1980-2000, then extend to 2005, 2009) to examine whether the price/elasticity of temperature risk has risen over time. Report Monte Carlo p-values and sensitivity to asset menu expansion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inference adjustments for beta estimation error (Shanken correction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjust cross-sectional inference for sampling error in estimated betas using Shanken (1992)-corrected standard errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report both uncorrected and Shanken-corrected t-statistics; rely on corrected statistics for significance claims about factor prices. Combine with Monte Carlo checks for further assurance.
